articles.title: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 Launches to International Space Station
articles.summary: Four crew members of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission launched at 11:10 a.m. EDT Thursday from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida for a science expedition aboard the International Space Station. “Crew-13 is another demonstration of America’s unmatched capability in human spaceflight and the strength of our commercial partnerships,” said […]
articles.content:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft launched on NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station with NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov onboard, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky

Four crew members of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission launched at 11:10 a.m. EDT Thursday from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida for a science expedition aboard the International Space Station.

“Crew-13 is another demonstration of America’s unmatched capability in human spaceflight and the strength of our commercial partnerships,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Jessica, Luke, Joshua, and Sergey will carry forward important work aboard the International Space Station while helping us build the experience and capabilities needed for ambitious missions to the Moon and beyond. Congratulations to the crew and the NASA and SpaceX teams who made today’s launch possible.”

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket propelled a Dragon spacecraft into orbit carrying NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. The spacecraft will dock autonomously to the forward port of the station’s Harmony module at approximately 7 p.m., making it the fastest launch-to-docking by a U.S. spacecraft in the history of the International Space Station.

“Our steady cadence of commercial crew launches demonstrates the essential role the International Space Station plays in sustaining our presence in Earth’s orbit and sharpening the tools we’ll take forward to the Moon and Mars,” said Dr. Lori Glaze, associate administrator of NASA’s Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “Each space station mission adds to our blueprint for exploration, and the work our crews carry out guides our plans while ensuring we keep pushing the boundaries of what’s possible in human spaceflight.”

During Dragon’s approximately 7-hour, 50-minute flight, SpaceX will monitor a series of automatic spacecraft maneuvers from its mission control center in Hawthorne, California. NASA will monitor space station operations throughout the flight from the Mission Control Center at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

NASA’s live arrival coverage begins at 5:20 p.m. for rendezvous, docking, and hatch opening. After docking, the crew members will change out of their spacesuits and prepare cargo for offload before opening the hatch to the station’s Harmony module around 8:45 p.m.

NASA will stream Crew‑13’s arrival across multiple platforms. Learn where to watch at:

https://www.nasa.gov/live

Watkins, Delaney, Kutryk, and Teteryatnikov will join the Expedition 75 crew, which includes NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina already aboard the station. After a brief handover, NASA’s SpaceX Crew‑12 mission, with agency astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, will return to Earth.

During its mission, Crew‑13 will help advance research aboard the orbiting laboratory by using microgravity to produce human stem cell‑derived tissues for improved personalized medicine, disease modeling, and pharmaceutical testing for conditions such as heart disease and Parkinson’s. The crew also will explore crop production through a new, mostly autonomous plant growth system and test how plants grow outside dedicated facilities. In addition, the crew members will continue human‑health studies that examine factors linked to blood-flow abnormalities in microgravity and will test a new inflight diagnostic device to monitor astronaut health.

Crew-13 is part of NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, which partners with private companies to provide reliable access to space, support research and development aboard the space station, and enable future missions beyond low Earth orbit.

Learn more about NASA’s Space Crew-13 at:

https://www.nasa.gov/mission/nasas-spacex-crew-13/

articles.personality_title: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 launches successfully to the International Space Station
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA regularly sends astronauts to the International Space Station (ISS) to conduct scientific research and prepare for future space missions. These missions often involve partnerships with private companies and international space agencies.

**What happened** – On October 1, 2026, four astronauts launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The crew includes NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. Their spacecraft, the Dragon, is set to dock automatically with the ISS the same day, making it the fastest docking by a U.S. spacecraft to the station.

**Impact** – This mission shows how NASA and its commercial and international partners work together to advance human spaceflight. The crew will conduct important experiments, such as growing human stem cell tissues to improve medicine and testing new ways to grow plants in space. These activities help scientists understand how to keep astronauts healthy and prepare for longer missions to the Moon and Mars.

**What's next step** – After docking, the crew will join the current ISS team to begin their research and maintenance work. The previous crew will return to Earth soon after. The data and experience from this mission will guide NASA’s plans for future space exploration beyond Earth’s orbit.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission successfully launched and docked with the ISS, advancing important science and international teamwork for future space exploration.
articles.personality_title_fr: La mission Crew-13 de SpaceX de la NASA décolle avec succès vers la Station spatiale internationale
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La NASA envoie régulièrement des astronautes à la Station spatiale internationale (ISS) pour mener des recherches scientifiques et préparer les futures missions spatiales. Ces missions impliquent souvent des partenariats avec des entreprises privées et des agences spatiales internationales.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 1er octobre 2026, quatre astronautes ont décollé à bord d’une fusée Falcon 9 de SpaceX depuis Cape Canaveral, en Floride. L’équipage comprend les astronautes de la NASA Jessica Watkins et Luke Delaney, l’astronaute canadien Joshua Kutryk, et le cosmonaute russe Sergey Teteryatnikov. Leur vaisseau, le Dragon, doit s’amarrer automatiquement à l’ISS le même jour, réalisant ainsi l’amarrage le plus rapide pour un vaisseau américain.

**Impact** – Cette mission montre comment la NASA et ses partenaires commerciaux et internationaux collaborent pour faire avancer le vol spatial habité. L’équipage mènera des expériences importantes, comme la culture de tissus dérivés de cellules souches humaines pour améliorer la médecine, et testera de nouvelles méthodes de culture de plantes dans l’espace. Ces travaux aident à comprendre comment garder les astronautes en bonne santé et préparer des missions plus longues vers la Lune et Mars.

**Prochaine étape** – Après l’amarrage, l’équipage rejoindra l’équipe actuelle de l’ISS pour commencer leurs recherches et travaux d’entretien. L’équipage précédent rentrera bientôt sur Terre. Les données et expériences de cette mission guideront les futurs projets de la NASA au-delà de l’orbite terrestre.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La mission Crew-13 de SpaceX de la NASA a décollé et s’est amarrée avec succès à l’ISS, faisant progresser la science importante et la coopération internationale pour l’exploration spatiale future.
articles.personality_title_es: La misión Crew-13 de SpaceX de la NASA despega con éxito hacia la Estación Espacial Internacional
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La NASA envía regularmente astronautas a la Estación Espacial Internacional (EEI) para realizar investigaciones científicas y preparar futuras misiones espaciales. Estas misiones suelen involucrar asociaciones con empresas privadas y agencias espaciales internacionales.

**Qué pasó** – El 1 de octubre de 2026, cuatro astronautas despegaron a bordo de un cohete Falcon 9 de SpaceX desde Cape Canaveral, Florida. La tripulación incluye a los astronautas de la NASA Jessica Watkins y Luke Delaney, al astronauta canadiense Joshua Kutryk y al cosmonauta ruso Sergey Teteryatnikov. Su nave, Dragon, se acoplará automáticamente a la EEI el mismo día, logrando el acoplamiento más rápido de una nave estadounidense.

**Impacto** – Esta misión demuestra cómo la NASA y sus socios comerciales e internacionales trabajan juntos para avanzar en el vuelo espacial tripulado. La tripulación realizará experimentos importantes, como cultivar tejidos derivados de células madre humanas para mejorar la medicina, y probar nuevas formas de cultivar plantas en el espacio. Estas actividades ayudan a entender cómo mantener saludables a los astronautas y prepararse para misiones más largas a la Luna y Marte.

**Próximo paso** – Después del acoplamiento, la tripulación se unirá al equipo actual de la EEI para comenzar su investigación y trabajos de mantenimiento. La tripulación anterior regresará pronto a la Tierra. Los datos y la experiencia de esta misión guiarán los planes futuros de la NASA para exploración más allá de la órbita terrestre.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La misión Crew-13 de SpaceX de la NASA despegó y se acopló con éxito a la EEI, impulsando la ciencia y la cooperación internacional para futuras exploraciones espaciales.

articles.title: NASA’s Webb Provides Crash Course on Planet-Shattering Collisions
articles.summary: In the early history of our solar system, scientists theorize that a Mars-sized object called Theia smashed into the infant Earth, vaporizing massive amounts of rock and blasting it into space. Some of that material coalesced into the Moon, where NASA’s Artemis program is returning humans, preparing for Mars, and shaping the future of space […]
articles.content:
In the early history of our solar system, scientists theorize that a Mars-sized object called Theia smashed into the infant Earth, vaporizing massive amounts of rock and blasting it into space. Some of that material coalesced into the Moon, where NASA’s Artemis program is returning humans, preparing for Mars, and shaping the future of space exploration.

That long-ago, violent collision reshaped our home planet. Astronomers have used NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope to examine a class of young stellar systems that show signs of similar upheavals, providing clues to the amount of energy in their collisions. The results offer insights into the composition and evolution of these chaotic systems.

The team’s findings published Thursday in The Astrophysical Journal.

Image: Extreme Debris Disk (Artist’s Concept)

The types of collisions within young stellar systems known as extreme debris disks are relevant to scientists’ understanding of our own solar system, which is thought to have undergone similar impact events that created our Moon and shaped Earth’s initial state. Artwork: NASA, ESA, CSA, Joseph Olmsted (STScI)

The environment surrounding a star changes as it ages, beginning with a juvenile, gas-rich protoplanetary disk where forming planets can reside, before evolving to a gas-poor debris disk. During its mission lifetime, NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope examined the debris disk stage and discovered a subclass termed extreme debris disks. These systems harbor unusually large amounts of warm dust close to the star, in the region comparable to where rocky planets orbit in our solar system. A team of astronomers led by Kate Su of the Space Science Institute in Boulder, Colorado investigated these intriguing objects with Webb.

Contrary to theoretical predictions, which suggest we should observe many extreme debris disks, observations indicate that these environments are rare. Scientists estimate roughly only 1% of young stars show observable signatures of this phase based on the data collected so far, including possibly our own solar system during its formation. Despite their rarity, the team was able to compile a sample of 21 extreme debris disks, including five from Spitzer’s archival data and 16 from Webb, with 12 newly observed disks and follow-up observations on four of Spitzer’s.

“This is the first time we have gathered enough systems to truly understand this subclass that we call extreme debris disks,” said Su, lead author of the paper. “Before Webb, we had limited information. We knew that they are weird and very different from the typical cold debris disks that we know, like Vega and Fomalhaut. Now that we have more data, we can pin down what these disks represent for planet formation and evolution.”

The team confirmed that extreme debris disks share three key properties: smaller dust grains than those in protoplanetary or classic debris disks, a high concentration of warm dust, and irregular brightness variations, all revealed by mid-infrared spectra from Webb and Spitzer.

To determine the driving factor for these qualities, the team studied the mineralogical makeup of the disks. They found that their sample could be categorized into silica-rich and silica-poor disks. Volcanic glass like obsidian is one example of silica-rich material found on Earth, whereas the silica-poor mineral forsterite appears as green sand grains on some beaches in Hawaii. An extreme debris disk’s category relays information on the type of collisions producing the impact debris and may help account for its variability in infrared brightness.

“To just see their mid-infrared emission and beautiful spectral features with Webb, which allowed us to identify their compositions, was the most exciting thing for me,” said Agnes Kospal of Konkoly Observatory in Budapest, Hungary, and a coauthor of the study. “We have no other way to study these planetary embryos directly because they are too small.”

Of their sample, about one-third is silica-rich, suggesting these disks are produced by high-energy impacts between Mars-sized bodies where a significant portion of the material is vaporized. The remaining two-thirds of their sample is silica-poor, indicating that the collisions are occurring on smaller scales, like grazing, between Moon-sized objects. Silica-rich disks are found only around stars younger than 300 million years, while silica-poor disks persist across a broad range of ages and often show greater brightness variability. The team proposes that this variability is driven by the rapid evolution of fresh debris through orbital changes and additional impacts.

Their findings can be applied to our own solar system, which may have experienced more than one extreme debris disk phase.

“How rocky planets formed and giant planets evolved are part of the broader story of the solar system’s formation. It’s all one story,” said Su. “Our work on extreme debris disks helps us bring together the big picture of what we currently understand.”

Image: Composition of Extreme Debris Disks Across Time

By investigating the compositions of extreme debris disks, scientists inferred that silica-rich disks are produced by high-energy impacts of Mars-sized objects, while silica-poor disks are created by less energetic events from Moon-sized bodies. Illustration: NASA, ESA, CSA, Joseph Olmsted (STScI)

Simulations suggest that terrestrial planets, such as Earth, should form within the first few hundred million years of a solar system’s formation. This period fits with the ages of silica-rich extreme debris disks observed so far and aligns with the estimation that Earth and the Moon formed around 100 million years after the Sun formed, with the Moon likely being the result of a collision between Earth and a Mars-sized object.

As for whether our Sun underwent a silica-poor extreme disk phase, if older silica-poor disks and their random intervals of infrared brightness do reflect orbital instability, this would be broadly consistent with the Late Heavy Bombardment hypothesis for our solar system. In that scenario, the gas giant planets migrated significant distances, gravitationally disrupting the orbits of smaller bodies and triggering catastrophic collisions that generated the short-lived, dust-rich phases observed in extreme debris disks.

“Of course, there’s many things we still don’t know about these disks,” said Attila Moor of Konkoly Observatory, a coauthor of the study. “We expect no silica-rich systems among older extreme debris disks. We only have three disks in our sample that fit that age criteria, so it’ll be nice to observe more of these systems to confirm our hypothesis.”

The James Webb Space Telescope is the world’s premier space science observatory. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

To learn more about Webb, visit:

https://science.nasa.gov/webb

articles.personality_title: NASA’s Webb Telescope Reveals Secrets of Planet-Shaping Collisions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists believe that early in our solar system’s history, a large object called Theia crashed into the young Earth. This collision sent a lot of rock into space, which later formed the Moon. Studying similar collisions helps us understand how planets and moons form.

**What happened** – Using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers studied 21 young star systems with unusual dust clouds called extreme debris disks. These disks show signs of big collisions between rocky bodies, similar to the one that created our Moon. The study, led by Kate Su, found two types of disks: silica-rich ones from high-energy impacts involving Mars-sized bodies, and silica-poor ones from smaller collisions.

**Impact** – This research is important because it gives us new details about how planets grow and change after huge crashes. For example, silica-rich disks appear only around younger stars, matching the time when Earth and Moon formed. The patterns of dust and brightness changes in these disks also help explain how debris moves and evolves after impacts.

**What’s next step** – Scientists want to observe more of these extreme debris disks, especially older ones, to confirm their ideas about how collisions shape planetary systems over time. This will improve our understanding of the early stages of planets like Earth.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Webb telescope has uncovered new clues about powerful collisions that shape planets and moons, shedding light on how our solar system formed.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le télescope Webb de la NASA révèle les secrets des collisions qui façonnent les planètes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques pensent qu’au début de notre système solaire, un grand objet appelé Théia est entré en collision avec la jeune Terre. Cette collision a projeté beaucoup de roches dans l’espace, qui ont ensuite formé la Lune. Étudier des collisions similaires aide à comprendre comment les planètes et les lunes se forment.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Grâce au télescope spatial James Webb de la NASA, des astronomes ont étudié 21 systèmes stellaires jeunes avec des nuages de poussière inhabituels appelés disques de débris extrêmes. Ces disques montrent des signes de grandes collisions entre corps rocheux, semblables à celle qui a créé notre Lune. L’étude, dirigée par Kate Su, a identifié deux types de disques : riches en silice, issus d’impacts très énergétiques impliquant des corps de la taille de Mars, et pauvres en silice, provenant de collisions plus petites.

**Impact** – Cette recherche est importante car elle donne de nouveaux détails sur la manière dont les planètes grandissent et changent après des collisions majeures. Par exemple, les disques riches en silice apparaissent uniquement autour d’étoiles jeunes, ce qui correspond à la période de formation de la Terre et de la Lune. Les variations de poussière et de luminosité dans ces disques aident aussi à comprendre comment les débris évoluent après les impacts.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques souhaitent observer davantage ces disques de débris extrêmes, surtout les plus âgés, pour confirmer leurs hypothèses sur la façon dont les collisions façonnent les systèmes planétaires au fil du temps. Cela améliorera notre compréhension des premières étapes de formation des planètes comme la Terre.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le télescope Webb de la NASA a révélé de nouveaux indices sur les collisions puissantes qui façonnent les planètes et les lunes, éclairant la formation de notre système solaire.
articles.personality_title_es: El telescopio Webb de la NASA revela secretos de colisiones que forman planetas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos creen que al principio de nuestro sistema solar, un objeto grande llamado Theia chocó con la joven Tierra. Esta colisión lanzó muchas rocas al espacio, que luego formaron la Luna. Estudiar colisiones similares ayuda a entender cómo se forman planetas y lunas.

**Qué pasó** – Usando el telescopio espacial James Webb de la NASA, astrónomos estudiaron 21 sistemas estelares jóvenes con nubes de polvo inusuales llamadas discos de escombros extremos. Estos discos muestran señales de grandes colisiones entre cuerpos rocosos, similares a la que creó nuestra Luna. El estudio, liderado por Kate Su, encontró dos tipos de discos: ricos en sílice por impactos muy energéticos con cuerpos del tamaño de Marte, y pobres en sílice por colisiones más pequeñas.

**Impacto** – Esta investigación es importante porque ofrece nuevos detalles sobre cómo los planetas crecen y cambian después de grandes choques. Por ejemplo, los discos ricos en sílice aparecen solo alrededor de estrellas jóvenes, coincidiendo con la época en que se formaron la Tierra y la Luna. Los cambios en el polvo y brillo de estos discos también ayudan a explicar cómo se mueve y evoluciona el material después de los impactos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren observar más discos de escombros extremos, especialmente los más viejos, para confirmar sus ideas sobre cómo las colisiones moldean los sistemas planetarios con el tiempo. Esto mejorará nuestro conocimiento sobre las primeras etapas de formación de planetas como la Tierra.

**Resumen en una frase** – El telescopio Webb de la NASA ha descubierto nuevas pistas sobre poderosas colisiones que forman planetas y lunas, iluminando cómo se formó nuestro sistema solar.
